title: My Pump.fun bot performs well on PAPER but badly LIVE — is ~500ms already too slow?
author: Competitive_Ant_9650
selftext:
I’ve been building an ultra-early Pump.fun trading bot.  
The basic flow is:  
CREATE → 50–160ms micro-flow check → BUY → monitor momentum → exit on the first meaningful drop / no-momentum.  
I’m using Helius + PumpPortal + Pump.fun.  
On PAPER some versions perform surprisingly well, but LIVE the results are much worse. My real BUY landing time is often around 400–600ms.  
I’m trying to understand whether the main problem is execution latency or if the strategy itself has no real edge.  
Has anyone tested something similar?  
Is 400–600ms already too slow for very early Pump.fun entries?  
Are flow acceleration / flow purity actually useful before entry?  
Does a FIRST-DROP exit make sense this early?  
How do you simulate realistic PAPER fills without accidentally creating fake profitability?  
I’m more interested in real execution data than backtest-only results.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: 500ms is not your main problem, the paper fill model is. on very early pump.fun entries the token you bought on paper at the create price got bought live by everyone else a couple hundred ms before you, so your real entry sits several steps worse up the bonding curve and your first-drop exit fires against a worse base. to make paper honest: only count a paper fill if a real transaction at or worse than your price landed after your order timestamp, and take that transaction's price as your fill, not the price you saw. then log your live entries against the paper entries for the same tokens. a constant gap means latency, a gap that grows with how good the paper trade looked means the idea itself. first-drop exits that early are mostly noise, one big wallet selling looks identical to the top. I built Quantradin for exactly the fill-honesty side, quantradin.com, costs nothing and stays on paper, but it is US stocks and options only so no help on solana. the rule above ports anywhere.

replies.author: Competitive_Ant_9650
replies.body:
Thanks, this is useful. One thing I want to clarify: for an ultra-early Pump.fun strategy, how would you implement the “honest” paper fill in practice?  
Would you replay the actual on-chain trades after my simulated order timestamp and use the first trade at or worse than my executable price as the fill?  
Also, how would you model the SELL side? My strategy enters very early and tries to exit on the first meaningful loss of momentum/drop. Should the paper exit also wait for a real subsequent transaction that proves my sell could have filled at that price?  
I have LIVE data with roughly 400–600ms landing times, so I can compare identical tokens PAPER vs LIVE. What metrics would you log to separate:  
latency/execution disadvantage,  
bonding-curve/slippage disadvantage,  
a genuinely bad entry/exit signal?  
And if first-drop is mostly noise this early, what would you measure instead to distinguish a temporary large-wallet sell from an actual momentum breakdown?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: yes, replay, with one tweak: add your measured latency to the order timestamp before you start scanning, then take the first trade at or worse than your price. same rule on the sell side, first trade at or below your ask after signal plus latency. expect the exit to eat more than the entry did.

replies.author: Competitive_Ant_9650
replies.body: I texted you on private can you accept me. Thank you!

replies.author: QuanTradin

replies.author: Competitive_Ant_9650
replies.body:
Thanks, I appreciate it. Your explanation about making the paper fills honest makes sense, and I’m implementing the latency-adjusted replay on both entry and exit.  
The bigger question I’m trying to answer now is whether I’m optimizing the wrong strategy. My bot is built around getting into very early Pump.fun launches as fast as possible, using small positions, and trying to capture the initial move before exiting when momentum starts breaking. In paper some versions looked very promising, but LIVE results have been much worse, which is why I’m now trying to separate unrealistic fills from an actual strategy problem.  
If you were in my position, would you keep this basic strategy and focus on improving selection + execution + the exit logic, or would you change the strategy itself? Especially since you mentioned that first-drop exits this early are mostly noise — I’m interested in what direction you would test instead.  
Also, this is my first bot and I’m building/testing it myself. Do you ever help with reviewing or improving existing code/strategies like this? Or do you sell a bot, system, strategy, or anything similar for Solana/Pump.fun?  
I’m not looking to start from scratch if I don’t have to. I already have the bot running in PAPER and LIVE canary — I mainly want to figure out whether the current idea can realistically be made profitable, or whether I should stop optimizing it and move to a different approach.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: honestly that's the real question. if the edge is being first into a launch, paper can't measure it, because on paper you never lose the race for the fill. live you're up against snipers on private RPCs who are faster than any retail bot. plot your live entry price against each launch's first trade and you'll see which race you're actually in.

replies.author: Competitive_Ant_9650
replies.body:
That makes sense. I can measure that from my LIVE runs.  
If I send you a sample of my LIVE logs showing CREATE detection time, send time, landing time/slot, my actual entry price and the first trades after launch, would you be willing to take a quick look and tell me whether I’m simply too late for this strategy to have an edge?  
My current landing is roughly 400–600ms. If that already puts me several trades behind consistently, would you personally abandon the “be first” approach and build the edge around selecting the right launches/momentum instead?  
Also, is private RPC / faster transaction routing realistically enough to close that gap, or are we talking about infrastructure that a small retail bot simply can’t compete with?  
And one last thing — do you do paid code/strategy reviews, or sell/build anything for Solana/Pump.fun? I already have the bot working, so I’d rather improve what I have if the underlying idea is still viable.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: sure, paste them here in the thread rather than DM. quickest check you can run yourself: count how many buys landed between CREATE and your fill. if it's always a dozen-plus and your entry sits well up the curve, the race is already lost at that latency and no exit rule fixes it.

replies.author: Competitive_Ant_9650
replies.body:
I found the PAPER vs LIVE results I was referring to.  
PAPER — V10.4 STOP A/B  
\- \~210 closed trades  
\- simulated net: +11.2125 SOL  
\- 86 wins  
\- \~41% WR  
\- \~7.12% ROI  
\- biggest simulated winners were roughly +2.95, +2.30, +0.94, +0.77, +0.72 and +0.60 SOL  
I then extended the test to around 440 trades and it was still about +10.2602 SOL simulated net.  
But when I moved essentially the same idea into LIVE CANARY, the edge disappeared.  
One of the V10.4.9 LIVE sessions had:  
\- wallet: 0.267879 SOL  
\- max position: 0.010 SOL  
\- max 5 trades  
\- REEF: -0.001483 SOL actual NET  
\- DCATPEPE: -0.002042 SOL actual NET  
\- after those positions the session was around -0.000516 SOL  
So this is the discrepancy I'm trying to understand. PAPER looked extremely profitable over hundreds of trades, while LIVE did not reproduce it.  
Based on what you said earlier, my suspicion is that the PAPER model was effectively getting fills it could never win in reality.  
If you were diagnosing this, would you first compare each PAPER entry against the actual on-chain trades at signal timestamp + measured live latency, then count how many buys landed before the first realistically executable fill?  
I'm especially interested in whether these results suggest:  
1. the PAPER fill model created most of the apparent edge,  
2. my \~400–600ms execution destroyed a real edge, or  
3. the underlying entry strategy itself doesn't have a LIVE edge.  
If useful, I can also paste a smaller LIVE transaction-level sample with CREATE/signal → send → processed/landed timestamps.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: add up those six winners: about 8.3 of the 11.2 SOL. so roughly three quarters of the paper result is six trades out of 210, and big winners on pump.fun are almost always the earliest entries, which are exactly the fills you lose to faster bots live. the other 204 trades are close to flat.

replies.author: Competitive_Ant_9650
replies.body:
Exactly — that’s the part I’m trying to isolate now.  
If \~8.3 SOL of the 11.2 SOL came from only six trades, then the key question is whether those six winners were still realistically executable after my measured live delay.  
My current live BUY lands roughly in the 400–600 ms range, while the paper replay is being changed to apply the measured latency first and only then take the first executable trade at or worse than the intended entry price. Same idea for exits.  
What I want to determine is: if I replay those exact six winners with a realistic 400–600 ms delay, failed/missed entries included, do they still remain large winners or disappear completely?  
If they disappear, then I agree the 11.2 SOL paper result is mostly an execution artifact and I should focus on reducing landing latency rather than optimizing the selection strategy. If some survive, then we can quantify how fast the execution actually needs to be.  
Would you agree that replaying those six trades individually with actual post-latency executable prices is the best next test?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: yes, one at a time. for each of the six log the post-latency fill, how many buys landed between signal and fill, and the exit you'd really get. if 4 of the 6 vanish you have your answer without touching the other 204.

replies.author: Competitive_Ant_9650
replies.body:
I went back through the full 210-trade run and checked the six largest winners individually.  
The six contributed +8.2901 SOL out of the +11.2125 SOL session net (\~74%), so they really are carrying most of the result.  
The timing is the interesting part:  
newsy: +2.3028 SOL paper, but BUY-1 → exit was only 98ms. By 98ms it had already moved +350%.  
PRINTER: +0.6014 SOL, BUY-1 → exit 147ms. It was already +111.5% by 143ms.  
PUMPone: +0.9434 SOL, BUY-1 → exit 171ms. It was +38.6% by 158ms and exited 13ms later.  
Paymunity: +2.9524 SOL, BUY-1 → exit 932ms, exit was triggered by a 1.4039 SOL dev sell.  
NOCT: +0.7223 SOL, BUY-1 → exit 1651ms, but it had already moved +51.6% only 131ms after signal.  
SXSN: +0.7678 SOL, BUY-1 → exit 2978ms.  
My measured live landing has been roughly 400–600ms. So three of the six — newsy, PRINTER and PUMPone — are already completely over before a live buy could even land. NOCT is still alive at that point, but the paper entry is clearly impossible because it was already +51.6% after 131ms.  
One limitation: this old logger did not persist every individual intervening trade, only aggregate pressure, so I can’t honestly give you the exact number of buys between signal and a 400–600ms fill or the exact post-latency fill price from this capture.  
But the timing alone already confirms the paper/live gap is material: at least 3/6 of the biggest winners are physically uncatchable at my measured latency, and a fourth (NOCT) is heavily repriced before I could land.  
So I think you’re right — the next replay needs to choose the first executable trade only after signal + measured latency, then run the exit from that actual fill rather than from the create-time paper price.  
Would you count NOCT as “gone” too given the +51.6% repricing before 131ms, or would you only classify the three that fully exited before my landing window?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: 98ms and 147ms exits against a 400-600ms live buy means those two never existed live, paper had already sold before your real buy would land. drop every paper trade that exits faster than your measured latency and rerun, whatever's left is the honest number.

replies.author: Competitive_Ant_9650
replies.body:
Exactly. That’s the issue I’m trying to eliminate now.  
I’m going to rerun the same frozen CREATE set and invalidate any paper trade where the exit happens before the measured live entry could have landed. For the remaining trades, entry will be the first executable trade at or worse than the paper price after the measured buy latency, and exit will use the same rule after sell signal + measured exit latency. Failed/missed entries will stay in the dataset too.  
Then I’ll compare the original paper PnL vs latency-adjusted executable PnL. That should tell me whether the edge survives real execution or whether most of it was coming from impossible sub-latency trades.  
Would you use each trade’s actual measured latency, or a conservative rolling p90/p95 latency for the replay?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: that's the right rerun. I'd write the latency number down before you look at any results, otherwise it's very tempting to nudge it until the six winners survive.

comments.author: LipTicklers
comments.body: Also needs slippage and fees which are the main things that eat this alive

comments.author: No_Bit_3377
comments.body: Could you clarify whether the 50–160 ms range includes the time your system spends checking the condition and sending the order? It isn't entirely clear what exactly is included in this time interval. If this represents your system's processing time—specifically condition capture/verification, triggering, order generation, and transmission—then that is a very long time. Your system should operate in the microsecond range internally; only then should you look into optimizing network latency.
